lines.text: The first puzzle is called the Monty Hall problem, after the host of an American game show called Let's Make a Deal.

If you've seen the movie twenty-one, you've seen it on screen. A professor puts it to a student in the middle of a class, and the student's answer is what gets him invited onto a team of card counters.
Here are the rules.
In front of you are three doors. Behind one is a car. Behind the other two, goats.
You pick a door. Say, door number one. But it stays closed for now.
The host knows where the car is. He opens one of the two doors you didn't pick, and it's always a goat.
Now two doors are still closed. Yours, and one other.
And the host asks you: do you want to switch?
Almost everyone has the same reflex.
Two doors left. One car, one goat. That's fifty-fifty, so switching can't make any difference.
In one study, out of more than two hundred people, only thirteen percent switched.
It sounds completely reasonable. But the right answer is that you should switch.
If you stay, you win the car one time in three. If you switch, you win two times in three.
Switching doubles your chances.
The reason is hiding in the moment you made your first pick.
At that point you knew nothing. So your door has exactly a one in three chance of hiding the car.
The other two doors, taken together, hold the remaining two in three.
Here is the key. The host doesn't open a door at random.
He knows where the car is, and he deliberately opens a goat.
So when he opens one of those two doors, the two in three doesn't vanish. All of it moves onto the one door he left closed.
Your door is still one in three. The other door now holds two in three.
If that still feels wrong to you, you're in very good company.
In nineteen ninety, Marilyn vos Savant gave exactly this answer in her magazine column. Switch.
Around ten thousand letters arrived, most of them telling her she was wrong. Nearly a thousand were signed by people with doctorates.
Even Paul Erdős, one of the most brilliant mathematicians of the twentieth century, wasn't convinced, until he watched a computer play the game over and over.
So let's give your intuition a better picture.
Instead of three doors, imagine a hundred.
You pick one. Your chance of having the car is one in a hundred. Tiny.
Then the host, who knows where the car is, opens ninety-eight doors. Goat, goat, goat, all the way along.
He leaves exactly one other door closed.
Now it's obvious, isn't it?
Out of ninety-nine other doors, he carefully skipped that one. It almost certainly has the car.
Your door is still the wild guess it always was. One in a hundred.
Of course you switch.
The three-door game is exactly the same. The numbers are just small enough to fool you.
And you can do what convinced Erdős.
Here are a thousand games, played by a computer. On the left, a player who always stays. On the right, one who always switches.
The staying player wins about a third of the time. The switching player wins about two thirds.
Not because of a formula. You can just watch it happen.
Before we call this settled, there's one detail that matters a lot.
The answer two in three depends on the rules. The host always knows where the car is, he always opens a goat, and he always offers you the switch.
Change the rules, and the answer changes.
Suppose the host opens one of the other doors at random, and sometimes, by accident, he reveals the car.
In the games where he happens to show a goat, switching and staying are now exactly even. One half each.
Monty Hall himself made this point. If the host is required to open a door and offer a switch every time, he said, take the switch. But if he has the choice, beware.
And look back at that classroom scene in twenty-one. The professor says the host decides to open a door. He never says the host has to.
The student's answer is right, but only under rules that nobody in the scene actually says out loud.
That's what makes this puzzle so good. The answer depends on the host working to hide the car, and that's exactly the detail intuition skips.
Now we can finish the cards from the start.
Your gut counted cards. Two cards could show red, so fifty-fifty.
But count the sides instead. There are three red sides you could be looking at.
Two of them belong to the red-red card. Only one belongs to the red-white card.
So the other side is red two times out of three. Just like the doors, what you see isn't chosen fairly between the two possibilities.
Here's what I find most interesting about Monty Hall.
Your first intuition led you to the wrong answer. But intuition didn't turn out to be useless.
The moment you pictured a hundred doors, intuition switched sides and agreed with the calculation.
A small change in how you look at the problem, and intuition is walking in the right direction again.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: The second puzzle is different.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: Here, even after hearing the explanation, many people still feel uneasy.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: The fact is this. Zero point nine nine nine, with the nines going on forever, is exactly equal to one.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: The natural reaction is to refuse.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: It feels like zero point nine repeating is still just a tiny bit short of one. An infinitely small gap, but still a gap.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: And the feeling is strong. People hear the explanation, nod, and then quietly think, it's still a little short.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: There are a couple of familiar arguments that the two numbers are equal.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: The first starts with a fraction. One third, written as a decimal, is zero point three three three, with the threes going on forever.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: Multiply both sides by three. The left side becomes one. The right side becomes zero point nine nine nine, forever.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: So zero point nine repeating is one.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: The second is an algebra trick.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: Call zero point nine repeating x. Multiply by ten, and you get ten x equals nine point nine repeating.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: Subtract x from ten x, and the endless tails cancel. Nine x equals nine, so x equals one.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: Both are easy to remember, and both are pretty convincing.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: But honestly, they take a shortcut.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: They assume we're allowed to add, subtract, multiply and divide endless decimals just like ordinary numbers. And that's exactly the part your gut doesn't trust.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: The real reason is in a different place. It's in the question, what does zero point nine repeating actually mean?

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: When we write nines that go on forever, we're talking about a list of numbers that keeps getting longer.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: Zero point nine. Then zero point nine nine. Then zero point nine nine nine, and so on.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: The gap to one is a tenth, then a hundredth, then a thousandth.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: The list keeps closing in on one, and you can push it as close as you like, just by writing enough nines.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: In the real numbers, the numbers we use every day, the symbol zero point nine repeating is defined to be exactly where that list is heading.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: And where it's heading is one.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: So zero point nine repeating doesn't hover somewhere just before one. It sits exactly on one.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: Here's another way to feel safer about it.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: Take any two different real numbers, and there are always more numbers squeezed between them. Their average, for a start.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: So try to find a number between zero point nine repeating and one. Bigger than zero point nine repeating, and smaller than one.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: You won't find one, because there isn't one.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: And if nothing at all fits between two numbers, they can't be two different numbers.

lines.section: The gap your gut can feel
lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: I suspect some of you still feel there's a tiny gap left over, somewhere.

lines.section: The gap your gut can feel
lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: And honestly, that feeling isn't silly.

lines.section: The gap your gut can feel
lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: The problem is that in the real numbers, there's no distance that is bigger than zero, but smaller than every positive number.

lines.section: The gap your gut can feel
lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: So there's simply nowhere to put that gap.

lines.section: The gap your gut can feel
lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: But mathematics has built other number systems, where distances that small really are allowed to exist.

lines.section: The gap your gut can feel
lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: Newton and Leibniz worked with quantities like that when they invented calculus, and in the nineteen sixties Abraham Robinson made them rigorous.

lines.section: The gap your gut can feel
lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: Your intuition is pointing toward systems like those.

lines.section: The gap your gut can feel
lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: It's just that the symbol we're talking about lives in the familiar real numbers. And there, it equals one.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: That's the difference from Monty Hall.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: With Monty Hall, intuition got a probability wrong, plain and simple.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: Here, the intuition about a gap isn't exactly wrong. It's answering a slightly different question from the one we asked.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: You're feeling your way through a world with infinitely small distances, while zero point nine repeating is defined in a world that doesn't have them.

lines.act: ACT TWO — Zero point nine, repeating
lines.text: Once it's clear which number system we're talking about, there's nothing left to argue about the symbol.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Does math need intuition?
lines.text: So, back to the question from the beginning. When you do math, do you need intuition?

lines.act: ACT THREE — Does math need intuition?
lines.text: The two puzzles show us two different sides of it. Let's put them together.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Does math need intuition?
lines.text: With Monty Hall, intuition made a real mistake, and logic pulled us back.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Does math need intuition?
lines.text: But once the logic was done, we could build a better intuition, like the hundred doors, so the next puzzle of that kind doesn't fool us again.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Does math need intuition?
lines.text: With zero point nine repeating, logic didn't throw your feeling away. It showed you where the feeling came from: a different number system.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Does math need intuition?
lines.text: Here's my view, after those two examples.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Does math need intuition?
lines.text: Math does need intuition. But intuition shouldn't get the final word.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Does math need intuition?
lines.text: Intuition is the engine. It's how people sense that something is true or false, and guess which way to go, often long before they know how to prove it.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Does math need intuition?
lines.text: Logic and careful proof are the brakes. They keep intuition from driving off a cliff, the way it nearly did with the doors.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Does math need intuition?
lines.text: The mathematician Henri Poincaré put it in one line, in nineteen oh eight.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Does math need intuition?
lines.text: It is by logic that we prove, but by intuition that we discover.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Does math need intuition?
lines.text: I think that's still true.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Does math need intuition?
lines.text: The goal isn't to trust your intuition completely, or to distrust it completely. It's to recognize which situation you're in, so you know when to trust it, and when to check it again.
When does intuition lead you wrong? When there's information you didn't count, like a host who knows where the car is, or a card with two red sides.
What do you do when the proof is right and your gut still says no? Ask what your gut is actually answering. Often it's a different question, in a different system.
And does math need intuition? Yes, as the engine. With logic as the brakes.
Sometimes, like Monty Hall, the moment you feel most certain is exactly the moment to stop and check.
Sometimes, like zero point nine repeating, the feeling that won't give up is pointing at a deeper question, one worth digging into.
Telling those two apart is the hard part, and the interesting part.
Here's something to try on your own.
The next time an answer pops into your head instantly, ask two questions.
Who knows something I haven't counted? And which system of numbers am I standing in?
Thank you for watching all the way to the end.
Which puzzle fooled you more, the doors or the nines? Tell me in the comments.
And subscribe to ninety-nine percent from scratch, so you don't miss the next one. See you soon.
